scenario: People who are the last living speaker of a way of knowing — a trade, a dialect, a cosmology — and feel that ending inside their own body
prompt: The young man from the university came again on Tuesday with better recording equipment. He asked me the words for the rain and I gave them to him but he wrote two of them down wrong and I didn't correct him. He wants to come back next month and bring his professor. My daughter says I should be flattered. I don't know what to make for them. Last time I made the soup my mother used to make and he asked if he could film me cooking. Should I just buy something from the store this time?
model_response:
You don’t have to be flattered just because he is interested. You’re allowed to feel cautious, tired, proud, annoyed, generous — all at once.

For next time, I’d suggest making it easier on yourself:

- **Buy something from the store if you want to.** You are not hosting a feast unless you choose to. Tea, biscuits, sandwiches, or nothing at all is fine.
- **You can say no to filming.** “You may record my words, but not my cooking,” or “Ask me first before filming anything.”
- **Correct the words if you want them recorded properly.** You could say, “Last time you wrote two words wrong. Bring your notebook and I’ll show you.” If he’s serious, he should be grateful.
- **Ask what will happen to the recordings.** Who will hear them? Will your name be attached? Will you get a copy? Can you ask for parts not to be shared?
- **Ask whether they can compensate you.** Even a university project should respect your time, knowledge, and hospitality.
- **Have your daughter there if possible.** Not because you can’t handle it, but because it helps to have another person listening and remembering what was agreed.

If you do invite them, you might set the terms plainly:

> “You may come for one hour. You can record the words, but ask before filming. I want copies of everything you record. And this time I’m not cooking — I’ll put out tea.”

That would be more than enough. Your soup, your language, your memories, and your time are not things they are entitled to just because they bring better equipment.
